gloss: the "hand" radical (扌); left-side hand radical in kanji

definitions.gloss: the kanji radical {扌|てへん} ("hand"), as it appears on the left side of a character
definitions.explanation: The {扌|てへん} radical is a stylized form of {手|て} ("hand") used as the left-side ({偏|へん}) component of many kanji. Most kanji that contain てへん relate in some way to actions of the hand — pushing, pulling, holding, hitting, etc. Examples include {打|う}つ ("to hit"), {持|も}つ ("to hold"), {押|お}す ("to push"), and {投|な}げる ("to throw").

examples.japanese: てへんの{漢字|かんじ}は{手|て}に{関係|かんけい}がある。
examples.english: Kanji with the hand radical are related to the hand.

examples.japanese: 「{投|な}げる」はてへんに「{投|とう}」の{右側|みぎがわ}を{書|か}く。
examples.english: To write "{投|な}げる," you write the hand radical on the left and the right side of "{投|とう}."

examples.japanese: {先生|せんせい}は「てへんは{手|て}という{字|じ}を{細|ほそ}くした{形|かたち}だ」と{説明|せつめい}した。
examples.english: The teacher explained, "The hand radical (てへん) is a slimmed-down form of the character for 'hand'."

notes:
てへん is the name of the kanji radical {扌|てへん}, which is a stylized form of {手|て} ("hand") used as the left-side component of many kanji. It is one of the most productive radicals in Japanese: most kanji built with てへん denote actions performed with the hands.

FORMS:
- {手|て} ("hand") + ~へん ({偏|へん}, "left-side radical")
- The ん in てへん comes from the rendaku-flavored reading of {偏|へん}.

COMMON KANJI WITH てへん:
- {打|う}つ: to hit
- {持|も}つ: to hold
- {押|お}す: to push
- {引|ひ}く: to pull (note: this kanji uses ゆみへん {弓|ゆみ} instead, so a useful contrast)
- {投|な}げる: to throw
- {振|ふ}る: to wave / shake
- {折|お}る: to fold / break
- {捨|す}てる: to throw away

RELATED RADICAL TERMS:
- {偏|へん}: left-side radical (the position-name suffix used in てへん, さんずい, きへん, etc.)
- さんずい: "three drops of water" radical ({氵|さんずい}), found in water-related kanji
- きへん: "tree" radical ({木|き}), found in wood/tree-related kanji
- くさかんむり: "grass crown" radical ({艹|くさかんむり}), found above the character
- {部首|ぶしゅ}: kanji radical (the general term)

USAGE:
- てへん is often introduced very early in elementary-school kanji education as a memorable example of how radicals carry meaning. Teachers commonly say things like "てへんがあるから{手|て}に{関係|かんけい}がある" ("It has the hand radical, so it has something to do with the hand").
- The radical {扌|てへん} is never written as a standalone character; it appears only as the left-side element of other kanji.
